<reason>Both sides ran coherent, well-grounded cases: PRO on dependency-ratio arithmetic and intergenerational burden-sharing, CON on unequal longevity gains and the un-aimable "gate." The decisive clash was PRO's reversal of CON's empathy argument—showing that recurring, regressive payroll taxes also land on the care aide every paycheck for forty years—and PRO's double-standard point that CON demanded surgical precision from carve-outs while its own progressive dial (cap-lifts) faced the same political friction CON dismissed. CON's counter ("the dial exists, the gate cannot be tilted"; "targeted relief admits the mean is the wrong ruler") was sharp and honest, and its refusal to invent a 2060 rate showed good epistemic discipline. But CON never fully resolved why a forever-recurring wage tax on the vulnerable beats small phased work increments on the generation that received longer lives. PRO made the burden comparison easier to decide. Both clipped turns (A1, A2) were minor execution costs.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's "empathy test" reversal in A2.2, later crystallized as the treadmill: CON's payroll alternative bills the same care aide on every paycheck for forty years while claiming to protect her, and the progressive dial CON touts requires the very political cap-lifts it accuses PRO of idealistically assuming. CON's strongest reply (B4.7, "she paid into insurance she could use") was responsive but did not neutralize the recurring-burden comparison.</best_rebuttal>
